zones.label: Column 1, part 1
zones.note: Lexical review aid: NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510, CC BY 4.0 (https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Consulted after independent scan reading; the transcription and review notes are this reviewer's work, not a reproduction of the index.

lines.note: Continues the preceding entry with favours from the king; the damaged word is Rey, not merely R. The final upright S. is the written-register label, outside the italic gloss.
Quǒxen is explained literally as yellow springs; the Portuguese begins the description of a place beneath the earth. Qina is one Japanese word, not the OCR fragments Q ina.

runs.text: terra, onde vão ter as almas dos que morrem,

lines.note: Completes beneath the earth and says that the souls of the dead go there. The clause belongs to the underworld entry, not to a geographical spring.
The compilers qualify the preceding account as what the non-Christian population believes. This attribution is part of the historical gloss, not an assertion by the reviewer.
The Japanese explanatory phrase means yellow paper, agreeing directly with Papel amarelo. The headword is continuous and the final S. is an upright register label.
Quǒ ya is paraphrased as a broad field. The scan retains a real gap before ya, unlike the spurious OCR gap after initial Q; the Portuguese continues eſpa-/çoſo across the physical rows.
Completes spacious and adds the sense of uncultivated, abandoned ground. The second physical division is deixa-/do, retained rather than joined.
Completes deixado em mortorio, describing ground left uncultivated or out of use. The short row is a genuine continuation of the preceding gloss.
The explanatory phrase identifies a yellow garment. The following relative clause specifies its use by Japanese Buddhist clergy; the damaged long-o mark is retained as a caron.

runs.text: veſtem os Bonzos de Iapão por cima doutro

lines.note: Explains that Japanese Buddhist monks wear this yellow garment over another garment. Iapão is Portuguese within the italic gloss, not a Japanese typeface-toggle term.
Completes doutro vestido, the underlying garment. This single-word continuation is kept on its own physical row.
The Japanese phrase describes light shining and the Portuguese gives radiance. Enlargement establishes an abbreviation tilde over e in Reſplẽdor; both headword long-o marks are carons.
This separate entry concerns yellowed leaves. Its final circumflex contrasts with the preceding headword's caron; the damaged explanatory form reads Qibamitaru, not Q ibamitaru.

runs.text: como as do outono que eſtão pera cair.

lines.note: Specifies autumn leaves about to fall, completing the yellow-leaf sense. No extra botanical identification is required.
Ra is one of the stated forty-seven Japanese syllables. The decorated R belongs to this headword and spans six physical rows; the OCR had omitted it and left only A. The spaced numerals are retained.
Completes the description of ra as a syllable of the Japanese alphabet. The adjacent ornament is the preceding line's enlarged R, not additional text on this row.
A second ra entry gives the Latin anatomical gloss for the penis. The small a is abraded but the residual lower strokes support Ra; this is separate from the enlarged syllabary entry.
Rabiǒ denotes a disease of the private parts, as the gloss continues below. The headword's initial R and damaged medial b correct the misleading OCR Babiǒ.
Completes partes secretas, specifying the affected anatomical region. It continues Rabiǒ rather than the new animal entry below.
Racco is the marine animal whose fur is described next. The visible initial is R, not OCR F; domar retains the printed joined spelling rather than silently introducing a word boundary.

runs.text: de cabelos q̃ pera qualquer parte q̃ os inclinão

lines.note: Describes the animal's hairs as yielding in whichever direction they are inclined. Both abbreviation signs over q are retained without expansion.
Completes the observation that the fur lies down when stroked by hand. The Japanese example begins a comparison with racco skin, retaining the printed word spacing.

runs.text: He homem q̃ facilmente ſe inclina

lines.note: Completes a phrase describing a person like that skin: someone who readily inclines to others' opinions. Fitogia contains the copular ending, not a separate headword.

runs.text: ao parecer de quẽ quer, & pera qualquer parte.

lines.note: Completes the metaphor of a pliable person who follows anyone's opinion in any direction. The tilde in quẽ is abbreviation, not a Japanese vowel mark.

runs.text: Hũa mezinha como maßa miuda em-

lines.note: Raccha is a medicine resembling fine dough or paste. The next line names tea as an ingredient; the printed em- is retained at the edge.
Completes the medicinal description by saying that tea enters into it. Cha is Japanese embedded in a Portuguese explanation and its upright type is restored.

Rachi first denotes a hedge or enclosure, then introduces a figurative expression for making matters clear. The scan shows the object-particle form Rachiuo, not Rachino; the e in the compressed Permet. is faint.

The Portuguese explains giving a clear account of things. A new example begins Rachino aita, continued below; unlike the preceding example, its particle is read no. The n is faint, so that distinction remains a chosen, nonblocking reading rather than a claim of an undamaged glyph.
Completes Rachino aita fito, characterized as straightforward and readily responsive to reason. The Portuguese verb is physically divided obe-/dece.
Completes obedience to reason, then introduces exceeding or breaking the enclosure figuratively. The headword repeated in the example begins R, not the OCR's N; l introduces the alternative yaburu.

runs.text: Quebrar a ley, & preceitos, ou ir

lines.note: Buru completes yaburu. The Portuguese explains the figurative expressions as breaking law or precepts, with another paraphrase continuing below.
Completes going against reason. The printed historical form is rezão, with e, rather than the razão used a few rows above.

runs.text: Hũa caſcazinha delgada que tem o

lines.note: This Racocu denotes a thin inner skin of bamboo, specified on the next line. The initial is R; the middle o is abraded, but the surviving sequence supports Racocu rather than OCR Facocu.
Completes the definition by locating the thin skin inside bamboo. It is not a general description of outer bark.
A separate Racocu names a particular kind of aguila. Enlargement shows dotted i followed by l, not OCR agulla; the short gloss supplies no further description of the named material or kind.

runs.text: Hũa laya de vestido de ſeda fina que

lines.note: Another Racocu denotes a kind of fine-silk garment. The following line identifies its royal wearers; the supplied short-s spelling in vestido is retained without a global st conversion.

runs.text: os Reis da China, ou de Iapão veſtẽ por cima.

lines.note: Explains that kings of China or Japan wear this garment over other clothing. The faint capital C in China is recoverable; veſtẽ retains the printed abbreviation tilde.
Racqio is glossed with the Japanese verb for settling down or reaching a conclusion. Vochitçuqu is a single upright Japanese form; the OCR's italic V was spurious.

runs.text: concluirſe algũa couſa de embaraço como de-

lines.note: Describes resolution of a troublesome matter, such as a lawsuit. The visible como replaces OCR cono; the abbreviation mark remains on u in algũa.
Manda completes demanda; the Japanese example says the lawsuit was settled. The scan supports xita, not aita, and Con- begins the Portuguese conclusion at the top of column 2.

The lawsuit was concluded; the next example concerns a fortress. The scan prints the full Concluiuſe despite Con- at the end of column 1, so the repeated beginning is preserved rather than silently deleted.
Completes the fortress example as surrender of the stronghold. Xeqen- begins the next example about the realm and must not be attached to the Portuguese gloss.
Completes the negative example: the realm has not yet become settled. Xenu is the negative of the verbal construction, not an independent headword.
Explains the unsettled realm as not yet pacified or free of wars and revolts. The entire line continues the same negative example.
Racqua is the falling of blossoms, explained by hana no chiru koto. The Portuguese mentions roses and continues with flowers below; cairẽ retains its tilde.
Completes the flower gloss and introduces the saying that a fallen blossom does not return to its branch. The apparent extra r after the ampersand was OCR noise.

runs.text: A flor caida nõe torna ao ramo. Vſaſe per

lines.note: Translates the fallen-flower saying and begins its figurative application. The abraded negative is retained provisionally as printed-looking nõe, rather than silently regularized to não; a tight but real space separates A flor.

runs.text: met. Acerca da idade, ou annos que paſſados

lines.note: Explains that the saying is applied figuratively to age or elapsed years. Per met. is divided between this row and the preceding one.
Completes the comparison: years once passed do not return. This short row finishes the application of the flower proverb.
Racu is equated with enjoyment and glossed as delights or pleasures. The noun is followed by two distinct verbal examples.
The alternatives suru and ukuru express enjoying or receiving pleasure. The gloss visibly reads Delitarſe, without supplying the additional vowel of modern deleitar-se.
Racuni fuqeru describes giving oneself over to pleasure. The Portuguese word for delights is divided delici-/as across the physical rows.
Completes delicias and adds pleasures, finishing the explanation of indulgence. The opening as is a word ending, not an article beginning a new gloss.
Racu asobi denotes recreation pursued freely and at one's ease. The initial R corrects OCR B, while the internal long s remains as printed.
The Japanese phrase explicitly means falling from a horse. The right edge prints the continuation mark after caua; the Portuguese words cair do are distinct.

Lo completes caualo; the repeated Racuba suru gives the verbal expression for falling from a horse. The abraded repeated headword is supported by its surviving strokes and the line above, not OCR Raotba.
Racubai concerns falling ume blossoms. The Portuguese describes the blossom of this tree rather than a fallen fruit; the tree comparison continues below.
Completes the tree description by comparing it to a plum tree. The abraded historical spelling ameixieira is retained, without importing a modern botanical name.

Racuchǔ means within the capital, paraphrased by Miyacono vchi. Miyaco is divided across the row boundary. The u bears a caron; only a faint remnant survives where the supplied Mi- division mark stands, so that mark remains a nonblocking uncertainty.
Completes Miyaco in the gloss, then begins a Japanese example of travelling around inside and outside the capital. The repeated Racuchǔ has a visible long-u mark, omitted by the OCR.
Mauaru completes the circuit-making verb. The Portuguese explains going throughout Miyaco; the printed joined portodo is preserved, and dentro is divided at the edge.
Completes dentro and adds outside, matching the contrast between racuchǔ and racuguai in the example.

runs.text: Racuda. Votçuru votçuru. i, Bǒzu zocuni

lines.note: Racuda is paraphrased by repeated falling and then by a monk's return to secular life. The Japanese explanation continues with cayeru below; the repetition is printed, not an OCR duplicate.
Completes the monk's return to secular status. The damaged Portuguese verb reads Fazerſe, including r; Ra- starts the repeated verbal example.
Completes Racuda suru, the expression for leaving religious status. This short Japanese continuation is not an independent entry.

runs.text: Certo modo de compor verſos, ou

lines.note: Racudai here denotes a particular method of composing verse, not an automatically imposed modern failure or examination sense. The definition continues with songs below.
Adds songs to verses as the objects of the composing method. The single-word row completes the preceding Racudai entry.
Racufat is explained as shaving off the hair. The scan contains the complete Raparſe at the right edge, not the OCR's truncated Raparſ-; the headword's final t is retained.

runs.text: a primeira vez, ou fazerſe Bonzo. Vt,

lines.note: Specifies the first shaving, or becoming a Buddhist monk. The next repeated example begins Ra- here and continues on the following row.
Completes Racufatſuru. The final-t stem and suru are joined in the print; no extra vowel or modern word division is supplied.
The Japanese identifies a descending wild goose, while the Portuguese calls it a wild duck. This lexical mismatch is preserved rather than harmonized; de- continues into dece below.
Completes descending or alighting below. The final upright S. is the register label, not part of the italic bird description.
The Japanese phrase means falling to the ground, matching the Portuguese exactly. The damaged headword vowel is a, not OCR i, and the final S. is upright.
Racugiacu concerns settling or determining a matter, expressed through ochitsuku. The printed space in Vochi tçuqu is retained rather than normalized to the joined form elsewhere.
Completes determining or passing judgment and gives the settled-lawsuit example. The small line-end mark after the Portuguese article A is visible and retained despite the unusual division.

runs.text: demanda està concluida, ou dada ſentença.

lines.note: The lawsuit is concluded or judgment has been given. The cedilla in ſentença is visible; the historical grave in està remains unchanged.
The Japanese example says one's deliberation has not yet settled. The negative Portuguese translation begins here and continues on the next row.
Completes not yet being resolved in one's opinion. This is the mental-decision sense of the same entry, contrasting with the lawsuit example.
Racuguai means outside the capital, matching Miyacono foca. The restored R and full Miyacono correct OCR losses; Miyaco in the Portuguese gloss is an embedded Japanese name.
Racuji denotes an omitted written character. The explanatory Iiuo represents ji wo under the dictionary's consonantal-I convention; it is not the OCR's long-s form ſiuo.
Completes the definition as a character not written through forgetfulness. The historical verb spelling eſcreueo is preserved.

runs.text: Racujit. Votçuru fi. i, Figa catamuqu.

lines.note: Racujit is sunset, explained by the descending or inclining sun. The scan separates fi. from the explanatory i,; OCR fiai merged these elements and incorrectly split the italic Portuguese ir-.

runs.text: ſe pondo o ſol, ou ſol que ſ vai pondo.

lines.note: Completes the sun's setting. The second reflexive element is visibly defective or abraded as ſ; the expected e is not supplied without surviving evidence.
Racujǒ denotes a surrendered or fallen fortress. The caron over o is retained; this is distinct from the preceding sunset entry.
The adverb means at one's pleasure or at ease. Aſeu retains the tight printed joining; the tall character is long s rather than the OCR's f.
Completes descansadamente and introduces passing one's time at ease. The edge prints Pa without a secure hyphen, so none is inferred before ſar below.

runs.text: ſar o tempo folgando, ou leuando boa vida.

lines.note: Completes the gloss as spending time in pleasure or living a good life. The initial ſar is the continuation of Pa, not the beginning of a new entry.
